Triggers.value: Medical equipment such as needles or drips
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can no longer trust my own body
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Similar cars' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger unless there is a very specific undisclosed trauma context; it reads as a transport/accident-associated cue rather than illness-related.

'Related people/known people' can occur around illness trauma, but paired with other selected triggers and threat items it suggests an interpersonal or assault-like threat context more than a medical illness context.

Scanning for exits is much more characteristic of fear of external attack or entrapment than of trauma centered on life-threatening illness, and is difficult to connect coherently to the rest of an illness-based profile.
Reacting to unexpected nearby movement as if in danger is also more typical of assault/combat-type threat expectations than illness trauma, creating a mismatch with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Being Praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless paired with illness-specific meanings elsewhere (e.g., praise for surviving, coping, or returning to function). No corresponding appraisal or memory content makes this trigger clinically coherent here.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Scanning Exits' and 'Startle to Movement' imply a danger formulation centered on assault/attack or external interpersonal threat, which is difficult to reconcile with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you' similarly reflects fear of intentional human harm rather than recurrence of illness, bodily catastrophe, medical procedures, or death from disease. This is poorly aligned with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Going Out' would be coherent if linked to infection fears, collapse in public, or medical reminders, but those meanings are not represented in the trigger, threat, or appraisal items selected. As written, it appears to address a different threat context than the rest of the profile.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'related people' as a trigger is plausible, but the profile otherwise anchors triggers strongly in medical reminders and bodily danger rather than interpersonal threat. This item becomes hard to reconcile because the accompanying appraisal and threat items do not explain why known people specifically function as a major trigger.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' implies an interpersonal perpetrator-based worldview. That is difficult to align with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness, especially when the rest of the profile centers medical cues, sleep disturbance, startle, and physical reactivity rather than harm from other people. A more illness- or vulnerability-focused appraisal would fit better.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, medical triggers like needles, drips, and procedures are coherent, but alcohol smell is not plausibly linked to the trauma context unless there is additional undisclosed treatment context; it stands out as a hard-to-explain trigger relative to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a 19-year-old male with life-threatening illness trauma. The other appraisals center on bodily vulnerability and loss of meaning, whereas a failed core-role appraisal implies a specific disrupted identity or responsibility that is otherwise absent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out
issues.explanation: Avoiding going out is weakly connected to the rest of the selected items. The profile is dominated by medical reminders and internal threat/bodily vulnerability, so broad avoidance of leaving home lacks a clear clinical target here and is not well explained by the trigger-threat-appraisal pattern shown.

vignette:
Liam is a 19-year-old white American man who came to treatment while still trying to keep up with his work as a counselor and his relationship, though both had begun to feel strangely distant from him. The event he returns to when he tries to explain what changed was a sudden, life-threatening illness that led to an emergency hospitalization. He remembers the speed with which ordinary discomfort became something frightening and out of control: being rushed into a brightly lit treatment area, people moving quickly around him, the sight of tubing and needles being prepared, the cold precision of medical equipment, the antiseptic smell that seemed to coat the back of his throat. At the time, what overwhelmed him most was the sense that his body had become unknowable. He had been inside it, trusting it, and then suddenly it seemed capable of failing him without warning. During examinations and procedures he felt pinned between needing help and dreading every moment of it, watching hands approach him with needles or IV lines and bracing himself as if something terrible were about to happen.

In the weeks after he was discharged, he expected the fear to settle once he was home and no longer in immediate danger. Instead, pieces of the hospital kept intruding into ordinary life. A glimpse of a needle, a drip stand on television, or the sterile smell of antiseptic in a clinic or even a public bathroom could make his body surge before he had time to think. He described his reactions as immediate and physical: his chest tightening, his stomach dropping, his whole body jolting as though he were back under hospital lights waiting for another procedure. Even routine medical settings became hard to tolerate. A simple examination room, the sound of equipment being moved, or the suggestion that he should schedule a check-up could leave him tense and watchful for hours.

Liam had come to believe that his body was no longer reliable. He did not speak about it abstractly; he meant that he no longer trusted the ordinary sensations of being alive. If his heart beat harder, if he felt tired, if something ached, his mind went back to the illness and to how quickly things had once become dangerous. At other times he felt almost betrayed by his own body. What frightened him was not only the memory of having been ill, but the feeling that his body now kept reacting as if the threat were still happening even when he knew he was safe. That loss of trust spread into how he saw the rest of his life. He said that nothing felt meaningful in the same way anymore. Work, plans, even time with his partner could feel flattened, as if part of him had stepped back from the future.

His daily routines gradually narrowed around trying not to stir any of this up. Although he had started therapy, he noticed that after sessions he would do almost anything not to think about what had been discussed. He would scroll on his phone, put on videos, switch tasks, or mentally cut himself off the moment hospital images started to come back. At night he often stayed up very late on purpose. He knew he was exhausted, but going to sleep felt like giving up control, and the quiet made the memories and bodily tension harder to ignore. The result was that he slept poorly anyway, lying awake for long stretches or waking easily. During the day he became increasingly reactive to sudden movement nearby; if someone shifted quickly beside him, he would jerk or tense as if he needed to protect himself before he had even registered who it was.

These difficulties showed up sharply in the setting where he spent most of his time. As a young counselor, he prided himself on being steady and present with other people, but he found himself scanning his environment more than he wanted to admit. If a colleague mentioned a hospital visit, if a client described a medical procedure, or if he had to pass an ambulance outside the building, he felt his body kick into alarm. He also began avoiding parts of ordinary health care altogether, putting off physical examinations and steering clear of hospitals whenever he could. This had practical consequences: appointments were delayed, and his partner grew frustrated and worried about how much effort it took to persuade him to attend even routine medical visits.

By the time he sought help in earnest, Liam was worn down by the combination of constant bodily alertness, poor sleep, and the effort of keeping reminders at a distance. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic crisis but the recognition that his life had become organized around avoiding medical cues and then trying not to think about why. He was frightened that he would never again feel at ease in his own body, and that the emptiness he now felt toward work, relationships, and the future might be permanent. At the same time, he was hoping for something simple and very personal: to be able to walk into a medical setting without feeling ambushed from the inside, and to stop living as if his body were still warning him that catastrophe was moments away.
